description: Fela Kuti (born Olufela Olusegun Oludotun Ransome-Kuti on October 15, 1938, in Abeokuta, Nigeria) was the multi-instrumentalist and bandleader who created Afrobeat — a fusion of West African highlife and Yoruba rhythm with American funk and jazz — and aimed it, song after song, at Nigeria's military rulers. Jailed by the Buhari government in 1984, he was released after twenty months; Amnesty International had named him a prisoner of conscience. He died in Lagos on August 2, 1997, of complications related to AIDS, the cause announced by his brother Olikoye Ransome-Kuti. name: Fred Below
description: Fred Below Jr. was a Chicago blues drummer born in Chicago in 1926 and deceased there in August 1988. He started learning music and playing drums at DuSable High School, where at about fourteen he formed a jazz band with Johnny Griffin and Eugene Wright. In 1952 Little Walter left the Muddy Waters band, Wells took his place, and Walter took over the Aces; as Little Walter and the Nightcats they became one of the leading electric blues bands in Chicago. In 1955 Below left the band for Chess Records session work, while continuing on Little Walter's records and hit records for Muddy Waters, Junior Wells, Chuck Berry, Bo Diddley, Jimmy Rogers, Elmore James, Otis Rush, and Howlin' Wolf. Tony Russell credited him as a creator of much of Chicago blues' rhythmic structure, especially its backbeat.

description: Friday, F. name: Family reunions
description: Annual (usually summer) gatherings of extended Black families — born from post-emancipation searches for kin separated by slavery — featuring traditional foods, matching T-shirts, ancestry teaching, and church services or picnics.

name: Funeral-home advertising church fan
description: A mid-20th-century Black print form: a folding paper fan on a wooden stick, with a devotional or portrait image on one side and a business advertisement on the reverse. Its heyday was tied to hot, unairconditioned churches; meant to be disposable, fans were saved, and the saved fan has been framed as a symbol of the midcentury African American death-related observance. The documented example: the 1968 'Freedom Fighters' fan created by Ferguson Funeral Home: paper, wood, and metal, depicting Martin Luther King Jr., John F. Kennedy, and Robert F. Kennedy, its reverse advertising its locations and services. It is held by The Sixth Floor Museum (object 2018.018.0001). The Bedford Calendar and Novelty Company also made such fans, though the 1968 fan's maker is cataloged as Ferguson Funeral Home itself.

name: Fuller Products Company

name: Fish Fry
description: The fish fry is a communal Black food tradition — hot oil, cold drinks, music, and a room full of people — and, in CultureTechLens research, an economic institution organized around church-basement plate sales and gatherings after church. During Jim Crow, when Black patrons were excluded from restaurants and Black churches from white philanthropy, the fish fry functioned as a bank — in one telling preserved in CTL's under-documented-topics study, 'a financial system that no white banker could touch' — and churches funded legal defense and organizing through plate sales. A local-history account from Tennessee gives the micro-economics: 30 pounds of whiting bought for $5.00, with the proceeds paying for a new school. CTL flags the gap directly: no quantitative or institutional study of the fish fry as an economic system exists.

name: Family Cookout
description: Family Cookout is recorded in the CultureTechLens graph as a Practice, Provisional, under project LIFE-001, sourced to CTL Thin Brief CTL-TB-000048, 'Family Cookouts' (2026-10-09). The brief calls the cookout infrastructure: a grill, a park permit, and word of mouth assemble three generations in an afternoon, without an institution running it. Cookouts gather extended family and neighbors in parks, backyards, and church lawns — the signature warm-weather assembly of Black Chicago — with the grill as ritual center: ribs, chicken, burgers, and hot links, and sides like potato salad, baked beans, and greens carrying family recipes across generations. Holidays concentrate the tradition: Juneteenth, Father's Day, Memorial Day, and Fourth of July gatherings anchor the summer calendar. Public parkland like Washington Park and the lakefront has long hosted the largest cookouts. Every claim is graded PROVISIONAL.

name: Fred Taylor
description: Former NFL running back drafted ninth overall by the Jacksonville Jaguars in 1998; played for Jacksonville (1998-2008) and the New England Patriots (2009-2010) and rushed for 11,695 career yards; co-host of The Pivot Podcast.

name: Farm Security Administration
description: The Farm Security Administration was a New Deal agency created in 1937, successor to the Resettlement Administration, charged with aiding poor farmers during the Great Depression. It is remembered above all for its photography unit, directed by Roy E. Stryker: a small team — among them Walker Evans, Dorothea Lange, Russell Lee, Jack Delano, and Gordon Parks — sent across the country to document American life. The unit outlived the agency's name, passing to the Office of War Information in 1942 and working until 1944. Its file, transferred to the Library of Congress in 1944, holds about 175,000 black-and-white negatives and around 107,000 prints — an extensive pictorial record of the United States between 1935 and 1944. The unit's Chicago work — Lee's 1941 South Side series and Delano's 1942–43 railroad photographs — supplies a foundational layer of CultureTechLens's Cited Photo Archive.

name: Funkadelic
description: Funkadelic is an American funk-rock band that grew out of the touring band George Clinton assembled behind his Plainfield, New Jersey doo-wop group, the Parliaments. When a contractual dispute cost Clinton the Parliaments name, the same musicians signed to Detroit's Westbound Records as Funkadelic — the guitar-driven, psychedelic counterpart to Parliament within Clinton's P-Funk collective: two distinct bands with overlapping membership under one leader. Funkadelic's self-titled debut appeared in 1970, and Maggot Brain (1971) became its defining early statement. After a move to Warner Bros., One Nation Under a Groove (1978) put its title track atop the R&B chart for six weeks and became the band's first platinum album; “(Not Just) Knee Deep” followed to number one in 1979. The original album run ended in the early 1980s. As part of Parliament-Funkadelic, the band entered the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1997 and received a Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in 2019.

name: Freddie Jackson
description: Harlem-born R&B singer whose smooth, gospel-rooted tenor made him the defining male balladeer of the quiet-storm era. Frederick Anthony Jackson was born on October 2, 1956, in Harlem, New York, sang gospel at White Rock Baptist Church, worked the New York club circuit, sang with the funk band Mystic Merlin, and paid dues as a background singer for Melba Moore before signing with Capitol Records. His debut album Rock Me Tonight (1985) was certified platinum, its title track spent six weeks at No. 1 on Billboard's R&B chart, and the ballad You Are My Lady became his signature song, earning him two Grammy nominations, for Best New Artist and Best Male R&B Vocal Performance. The follow-up, Just Like the First Time, also went platinum, and across his career he accumulated ten No. 1 R&B singles, among them Tasty Love, Have You Ever Loved Somebody, and Jam Tonight. Jackson died on October 5, 2026, three days after his 70th birthday; no cause of death was disclosed, and he had spoken publicly in 2024 about living with kidney disease.

name: Founding of the NAACP (1909)
aliases: NAACP Founded; The Niagara Movement Succession
description: On February 12, 1909 — the centenary of Abraham Lincoln's birth — a group of Black and white activists issued 'The Call' for a national conference on the state of Black civil rights, answering the 1908 race riot in Springfield, Illinois, Lincoln's own hometown, which had exposed how far the nation had drifted from emancipation's promises. The conference met in New York that spring, and the organization it built — the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People — adopted its name in 1910 and grew into the central legal and lobbying instrument of the long civil rights movement. W. E. B. Du Bois (CTL-E-1484), a signer of the Call and the organization's director of publications and research, founded its magazine The Crisis in 1910. The NAACP itself is held at CTL-E-0498 (with the Chicago Branch at CTL-E-0286); this record holds the founding as an event, the moment the movement acquired its permanent institution. Through the Legal Defense Fund's predecessor work inside the association, the NAACP's lawyers carried the case load — Buchanan, Gaines, Sweatt, Brown — that dismantled Plessy piece by piece.

name: Freedom Rides (1961)
description: On May 4, 1961, thirteen riders — Black and white, organized by the Congress of Racial Equality (CORE, CTL-E-1187) — boarded buses in Washington, D.C., bound for New Orleans, to test whether the Supreme Court's rulings against segregation in interstate travel would be honored in the Deep South. In Anniston, Alabama, one bus was firebombed; in Birmingham, riders were beaten by a mob while police absented themselves; in Montgomery, a riot at the Greyhound station left riders and a federal observer injured and drew federal marshals. When injuries forced CORE to pause, Nashville students — SNCC's generation (CTL-E-5421) — took the seats and rode on to Jackson, Mississippi, where they were arrested and sent to Parchman Penitentiary rather than pay fines. More than four hundred riders ultimately joined. That November, under pressure, the Interstate Commerce Commission issued regulations with teeth, and segregation in interstate terminals ended in law as it had been broken in fact. The rides began, fittingly for this graph, with an organization founded in Chicago: CORE had been established there in 1942.

name: Freedom Summer (1964)
aliases: Mississippi Freedom Summer; Freedom Summer Project
description: In the summer of 1964, some one thousand volunteers — most of them white Northern college students — joined Black Mississippi organizers in the Freedom Summer project, a campaign coordinated by the Council of Federated Organizations to register Black voters in the state where only about seven percent of eligible Black citizens were on the rolls, and to build Freedom Schools and community centers alongside the registration drive. Before the summer properly began, on June 21, 1964, three project workers — James Chaney, a Black Mississippian with CORE; Andrew Goodman, a summer volunteer; and Michael Schwerner, a CORE organizer — were arrested by a Neshoba County deputy, released into the night, and murdered by Ku Klux Klan members near Philadelphia, Mississippi. Their bodies were found in an earthen dam on August 4, after a search that drew the FBI into Mississippi in force. The summer's other harvest was political: the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party, built by the project's organizing, challenged the seating of the state's all-white delegation at the Democratic National Convention that August, and Fannie Lou Hamer's testimony carried Mississippi's reality into America's living rooms.

name: Frank Marshall Davis
description: Frank Marshall Davis (December 31, 1905 – July 26, 1987) was a poet and journalist of the Black Chicago Renaissance. Born in Arkansas City, Kansas, he studied journalism at Friends University and Kansas State Agricultural College without graduating, and moved to Chicago in 1927 to work for Black newspapers. In 1931 he became managing editor of the Atlanta World, which he built into the Atlanta Daily World, the nation's first successful Black daily newspaper. Back in Chicago he served as executive editor of Claude Barnett's Associated Negro Press (1935–1947) and published the poetry volumes Black Man's Verse (1935), I Am the American Negro (1937), Through Sepia Eyes (1938), and 47th Street (1948), the last a chronicle of South Side life. A founding member of the South Side Writers Group, he lectured widely, taught jazz history, and was surveilled by the FBI until 1963. In 1948 he moved to Honolulu, where he wrote the 'Frankly Speaking' column for the Honolulu Record; his memoir Livin' the Blues appeared posthumously in 1992.

name: Fenton Johnson
description: Fenton Johnson (May 7, 1888 – September 17, 1958) was a Chicago poet, editor, and educator, a forerunner of the Harlem Renaissance who stayed home and built in Chicago. Born into a prosperous Black Chicago family — his father was a railroad porter — he attended Northwestern University and the University of Chicago and took a journalism degree from Columbia's Pulitzer School. In the 1910s he self-published three collections — A Little Dreaming (1913), Visions of the Dusk (1915), and Songs of the Soil (1916) — mixing lyric verse with the dialect poetry and early prose poems, like the bitter 'Tired,' that made his reputation; James Weldon Johnson called him one of the first Negro revolutionary poets. He founded two Chicago magazines, The Champion (1916) and The Favorite Magazine (1918–1919), and collected his stories as Tales of Darkest America (1920). In the 1930s he worked for the Federal Writers Project in Chicago, in the unit Arna Bontemps directed. He died in Chicago in 1958.

name: Fanum
description: Fanum (Roberto Escanio, born August 22, 1997, in the Bronx, New York City) is a Dominican-American streamer and content creator, and a founding member of the AMP (Any Means Possible) collective. He began streaming on Twitch in 2016, building an audience on GTA Online roleplay and New York-rooted vlog content, and originated the slang term 'Fanum tax' — his running bit of taking a cut of any food brought on stream — which entered youth vernacular far beyond his own channels. Fanum won Breakout Streamer of the Year at the 13th Streamy Awards in August 2023 and Best Roleplay Streamer at the 2022 and 2023 Streamer Awards. Platform-reported figures in 2026 put him at about 4 million Twitch followers and 3.9 million YouTube subscribers. CultureTechLens profiled Fanum in Short #92, published October 13, 2026.

name: Funny Marco
description: Funny Marco (Marco Summers) is a Kansas City, Missouri-born comedian and interviewer, now based in Atlanta, whose deadpan celebrity interview series Open Thoughts became one of digital comedy's signature formats. Summers built his audience on viral sketches before Open Thoughts put him across from guests including Kevin Hart, Nicki Minaj, and John Cena, holding a straight face through deliberately awkward questions. He extended the format to sports media with Marco Is Off the Ball on Bleacher Report and Max, a spoof of NBA post-game press conferences, and tours nationally with a live Open Thoughts show. Promoter biographies credit him with more than 14 million followers across platforms. CultureTechLens profiled Funny Marco in Short #94, published October 13, 2026.

name: Flavor Flav
description: Flavor Flav, born William Jonathan Drayton Jr. on March 16, 1959, in Roosevelt, New York, is an American rapper and hype man, and a founding member, alongside Chuck D, of Public Enemy. Raised in Freeport, Long Island, he taught himself piano, drums and guitar as a child, attended culinary school, and met Carlton Ridenhour at Adelphi University, where the two first collaborated on college radio. Within Public Enemy he served as the comic counterweight to Chuck D's somber delivery — the jester to the frontman's baritone — popularizing the role of the hype man, with signature oversized clock necklaces and the call 'Yeah, boyeee!'; he took the lead on the group single '911 Is a Joke' (1990). Public Enemy earned six Grammy Award nominations, and he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame as a member of the group. Biographical accounts document periods of addiction and legal trouble that interrupted his career in the 1990s. He returned to wide public attention in the 2000s as the star of the VH1 reality series The Surreal Life, Strange Love and Flavor of Love, and released a self-titled solo album in 2006. He remains an active performer with Public Enemy.

name: Fugees
description: The Fugees were an American hip-hop group whose members — rapper, singer and producer Wyclef Jean, rapper and singer Lauryn Hill, and rapper Pras Michel — took the group's name from the word refugee; Jean and Michel are Haitian American, and Hill is American. Formed in New Jersey after Jean, Michel and Hill began working together around 1990, the trio released Blunted on Reality in 1994 to little mainstream attention. Their second album, The Score (1996), became one of the biggest hits of its year and one of the best-selling hip-hop albums of all time, built on reinterpretations including 'Killing Me Softly' and 'No Woman, No Cry' alongside the original singles 'Fu-Gee-La' and 'Ready or Not.' At the 1997 Grammy Awards the group won Best Rap Album for The Score and Best R&B Performance by a Duo or Group with Vocal for 'Killing Me Softly,' and The Score was nominated for Album of the Year, the first such nomination for a hip-hop group. The members separated for solo projects in 1997: Hill recorded The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill, Jean launched The Carnival, and Michel scored a hit with 'Ghetto Supastar.' Lauryn Hill already holds a record in this graph (CTL-E-5565).

name: Flipmode Squad
description: Flipmode Squad is the Brooklyn hip-hop collective formed and fronted by Busta Rhymes. Busta Rhymes first introduced the name in 1993, while he was still a member of Leaders of the New School, with an early lineup built around Rampage; the best-known lineup — Busta Rhymes, Rampage, Lord Have Mercy, Rah Digga, Baby Sham and Spliff Star — first appeared together as Flipmode Squad on his album The Coming in 1996. The crew released its debut, The Imperial Album, on Elektra in 1998, and members balanced crew work with solo releases, among them Rampage's Scouts Honor... by Way of Blood (1997) and Rah Digga's Dirty Harriet. In 2000 the camp moved to J Records, and Lord Have Mercy left the Squad to pursue a solo career. A second crew album, Rulership Movement, is listed in AllMusic's discography as a 2002 J Records release; the group's history as carried by Wikipedia says it was set for 2003 and never released after a label change. That conflict is shown in this packet, not resolved. The Flipmode name and roster later fed into Busta Rhymes's successor camp, The Conglomerate.

name: Field Foundation of Illinois
description: The Field Foundation of Illinois is a Chicago philanthropy supporting organizations across Chicago, with grantmaking that Inside Philanthropy describes as investing in the city's local news outlets, organizers, arts, and creative expression as a form of community power-building. Its lineage runs to the Field Foundation established in 1940 by Marshall Field III, the Chicago banker and Chicago Sun-Times publisher, which supported organizations promoting civil rights, civil liberties, and child welfare and other groups working for social change, with grantee files documenting civil rights groups including the NAACP and the Southern Christian Leadership Conference. In 1960 the foundation split, and the Field Foundation of Illinois was established under the leadership of Marshall Field IV to focus its efforts locally in Chicago. In recent decades the Illinois foundation has been overseen with Marshall Field V serving as a board member and life director. Its best-known current initiative, Leaders for a New Chicago, run in partnership with the MacArthur Foundation, awards $50,000 each to Chicago leaders working in arts and culture, journalism and storytelling, and justice and community power building; beginning in January 2023 the foundation moved toward larger multi-year grants and what its leadership calls mutual accountability for resident-set agendas.

name: Fritz Pollard
aliases: Frederick Douglass Pollard; Frederick Douglass "Fritz" Pollard
description: Frederick Douglass 'Fritz' Pollard (January 27, 1894 – May 11, 1986) was a Chicago-born football pioneer who broke professional football's color line as player and coach. An All-America halfback at Brown University, he led Brown to the Rose Bowl and, per ESPN's account of his Hall of Fame induction, was the first Black player in the Rose Bowl, in 1916. After Army service in World War I he joined the Akron Pros in 1919; in 1920 the Pros entered the newly founded American Professional Football Association, soon renamed the National Football League, and went undefeated (8-0-3) to win the league's first championship. The Pro Football Hall of Fame records the precise firsts: Pollard was one of just two African Americans in the new league in 1920, and in 1921 he became the first African-American head coach in NFL history as co-coach of the Pros. He played and sometimes coached for four NFL teams, and in 1928 he organized and coached the Chicago Black Hawks, an all-African-American professional team. He was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2005.

name: Fay Young
aliases: Frank A. Young; Frank Albert Young; Frank "Fay" Young; John Lake Caution Jr.
description: Fay Young was the byline of Frank Albert Young (born John Lake Caution Jr., October 19, 1884, Williamsport, Pennsylvania – October 27, 1957, Chicago), the Chicago Defender sportswriter known to his peers as the Dean of Negro Sportswriters; his nickname 'Fay' came from the initials of his adopted name, F.A.Y. Working as a railroad dining-car waiter, he helped distribute the young Defender and reported news gathered on his routes before joining its staff as a volunteer in the paper's formative years; his bylined sports articles appeared from about 1912. He developed the Defender's sports page — an innovation other Black papers copied — became its sports editor, and also served as the paper's business manager by 1916 and managing editor by the late 1920s, with an interval as managing editor of the Kansas City Call in the 1930s. His columns included 'Fay Says,' begun in 1921, and 'Through the Years.' He covered the Negro Leagues from the Negro National League's founding in 1920, served as an officer of the Negro American League from 1937, and argued in print from the mid-1920s that Major League Baseball's color ban should be removed.

name: Fats Waller
description: Fats Waller (Thomas Wright Waller, born May 21, 1904, New York City; died December 15, 1943, near Kansas City, of pneumonia, aboard a train) was the stride pianist, organist, composer, and comic entertainer whose playing laid much of the basis for modern jazz piano. A student of James P. Johnson, he was a professional organist at fifteen and made his first recordings in October 1922 for Okeh. Waller copyrighted more than 400 songs, many written with lyricist Andy Razaf, including “Ain't Misbehavin'” (1929, written for the revue Connie's Hot Chocolates) and “Honeysuckle Rose.” From 1934 he recorded with his small band, Fats Waller and His Rhythm, and his wit at the keyboard made him a radio and film presence as well as a hitmaker. The 1978 Broadway revue Ain't Misbehavin' built a hit show from his catalog a generation after his death at thirty-nine.

name: Fernando Tatís Jr.
description: Fernando Tatís Jr., born 2 January 1999 in San Pedro de Macorís, Dominican Republic, is the San Diego Padres' right fielder and the son of former major leaguer Fernando Tatís. He debuted in 2019 and quickly became one of the game's most dynamic players, leading the National League with 42 home runs in 2021 and signing a 14-year, $340 million contract that February. In August 2022, Major League Baseball suspended him 80 games under the Joint Drug Prevention and Treatment Program after a positive test for Clostebol. He returned in 2023, moved to right field and won Gold Glove and Platinum Glove honors for his defense. In 2026 he remained San Diego's lineup fixture — 25 home runs, 83 RBI and a team-leading 38 stolen bases — and played right field through the Padres' October run to the Division Series. CTL stages him as an Afro-Dominican ballplayer; individual descent documentation is named as a gap below.

name: Floyd Mayweather Jr.
aliases: Floyd Joy Mayweather Jr.; Floyd Joy Sinclair; Money; Pretty Boy
description: Floyd Mayweather Jr. (born Floyd Joy Sinclair on 24 February 1977 in Grand Rapids, Michigan) is an American former professional boxer and promoter who retired undefeated and is regarded as one of the finest defensive fighters in boxing history. Born into a boxing family — his father, Floyd Mayweather Sr., was a welterweight contender who trained him, and his uncle Roger Mayweather was a world champion — he won three National Golden Gloves titles and a bronze medal at the 1996 Atlanta Olympics before turning professional that year. He won world championships in five weight divisions, from super featherweight to light middleweight, defeating among others Oscar De La Hoya (2007), Canelo Álvarez (2013) and Manny Pacquiao (2015), the richest bout in boxing history. He retired in August 2017 after stopping Conor McGregor, closing his professional record at 50 wins, no losses, 27 by knockout, and was inducted into the International Boxing Hall of Fame in 2021. Since retiring he has boxed a series of exhibitions; a much-publicized 2026 exhibition with Mike Tyson and a professional rematch with Pacquiao were both announced and then postponed during 2026, leaving his professional record untouched.

name: Floyd Mayweather Sr.
aliases: Floyd Joy Mayweather; Big Floyd; Floyd Mayweather
description: Floyd Mayweather Sr. (born Floyd Joy Mayweather on 19 October 1952 in Amory, Mississippi) is an American former professional welterweight boxer and one of boxing's most influential trainers. Fighting from the mid-1970s to 1990, he compiled 28 wins, 6 losses and 1 draw, was noted for defensive skill, and won a U.S. Championship Tournament contest in 1977. In 1978 Sugar Ray Leonard stopped him in the tenth round, and months later he was shot in the leg in a family dispute while holding his infant son, an injury that curtailed his career. He taught that son, Floyd Mayweather Jr., to box from toddlerhood and served as his trainer and manager — a tenure interrupted by a 1993 cocaine-trafficking conviction and a five-and-a-half-year federal prison sentence, a falling-out in 2000, and a reunion in 2013. Preaching defense, a stiff jab and the shoulder roll, he also trained Oscar De La Hoya from 2001 to 2006, as well as Chad Dawson, Joan Guzman and Laila Ali. He is living, reported in 2026 coverage as retired from full-time training and only fleetingly overseeing duties at the Mayweather gym in Las Vegas.

name: Florence Price
aliases: Florence Beatrice Price; Florence B. Price; Florence Beatrice Smith Price
description: Florence Beatrice Price, born April 9, 1887, in Little Rock, Arkansas, was a composer, pianist, organist, and teacher trained at the New England Conservatory, one of the few such schools then admitting Black students, where she earned diplomas in organ and piano teaching. After teaching in Arkansas and heading the music department at Clark University in Atlanta, she returned to Little Rock, married, and raised a family as racial violence intensified around her. In 1927, following a lynching in Little Rock, she moved to Chicago, and there her composing deepened into large forms. Her Symphony No. 1 in E minor won first prize in the 1932 Wanamaker competition, and on June 15, 1933, Frederick Stock and the Chicago Symphony Orchestra premiered it, making Price the first Black woman to have a symphony performed by a major American orchestra. Her music joins European Romantic practice to spirituals, call-and-response, and the juba dance. She wrote more than 300 works, many unpublished at her death in Chicago on June 3, 1953; manuscripts rediscovered in 2009 in her former summer home have driven a major revival.

name: Fannie Lou Hamer
description: Fannie Lou Hamer, born Fannie Lou Townsend on 6 October 1917 in Montgomery County, Mississippi, was an African American voting-rights and women's-rights leader. The youngest of twenty children of sharecroppers, she worked the fields from age six, received a sixth-grade education, and married Perry 'Pap' Hamer. In August 1962 she attended an SNCC meeting in Ruleville and volunteered to register to vote; she was fired from the plantation where she lived and worked, and became an SNCC field secretary, registering herself in 1963. She survived threats, shots fired into homes where she stayed, and a severe beating in a Mississippi jail in 1963. In 1964 she co-founded the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party and, as its vice-chair, testified before the credentials committee at the Democratic National Convention, describing that beating on national television; she also helped organize Freedom Summer. She later founded the Freedom Farm Cooperative and, in 1971, co-founded the National Women's Political Caucus. Hamer died of cancer on 14 March 1977 in Mound Bayou, aged 59. President Biden posthumously awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom in January 2025.

name: FunnyMike
aliases: MacArthur Johnson; 22 Savage; Young 22; Mighty Mike
description: MacArthur Johnson, born 8 October 1996 in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, is an American comedian, YouTube creator and rapper known as FunnyMike. An African-American creator raised in Baton Rouge and educated at Tara High School, he first posted short comedy clips on Vine before launching his self-titled YouTube channel in 2016, built on pranks, challenges and family videos. As a rapper he first drew national attention in 2016 as 22 Savage, a persona modelled on 21 Savage, releasing the single "No Heart" that August and announcing a Savage Mode mixtape; in February 2017 he renamed the persona Young 22. With his partner Jaliyah Monet he ran the joint MJ Family channel; their daughter Londyn was born in February 2019 and their son MacArthur Jr. in July 2020. He leads the Tha Bad Kids creator collective, whose comedy series reached a seventeenth season on streaming listings in 2025 and 2026.

name: Frank Wickware
aliases: Frank Ellis Wickware; Rawhide Wickware; The Red Ant; Smokey Wickware; Big Red Wickware
description: Frank Ellis Wickware (March 18, 1888 – November 2, 1967) was a Negro leagues pitcher celebrated for a dominant fastball in Black baseball's pre-league and early league years. The Society for American Baseball Research gives his birthplace as Girard, Kansas, while the Negro Leagues Baseball Museum gives Coffeyville, Kansas, the town his family later moved to; this record shows both rather than blending them. Rube Foster hired him for the Chicago Leland Giants in 1910, and SABR reports an unofficial 18–1 record for Wickware that season on a team SABR describes as going 123–6. He pitched for Foster's Chicago American Giants and for many other leading Black clubs, led the Cuban winter league with 10 victories for the Fe club in 1912, and in October 1913 defeated Walter Johnson 1–0 in Schenectady in a game shortened by darkness. On August 26, 1914, pitching for the American Giants in Chicago, he came within a leadoff walk of a perfect game against the Indianapolis ABCs. SABR notes that he was considered for the National Baseball Hall of Fame's 2006 Negro leagues special election, was inducted into the Kansas Baseball Hall of Fame in 2011, and died in Schenectady, New York, in 1967.

name: Federation of Black Cowboys
aliases: New York City Federation of Black Cowboys; FBC
description: The Federation of Black Cowboys is a New York City organization dedicated to horsemanship training, children's education, and keeping alive the traditions of African American cowboys of the Old West. Formed in 1994, it was based for years at the Cedar Lane Stables in Queens, on land owned by the city's Parks Department near the road to Kennedy Airport. Through youth programs, rodeos, school visits, and public appearances, it introduces city children to the legacy of Black cowboys, and uses horsemanship to teach life skills including patience, kindness, and tolerance. In 2012 six horses died at the Cedar Lane Stables, forcing the city to close the stables while the Federation renovated them. The Federation's last Cedar Lane licensing agreement was for 2015; in February 2016 it was informed its license would not be renewed after being outbid by GallopNYC, a nonprofit providing therapeutic horsemanship, although city officials acknowledged the Federation's positive historical contribution to the community and to horse riding in New York City. As of 2019 its president was Kesha “Mama” Morse, the organization's first female president, and in 2022 the Federation took part in Juneteenth programming in Manhattan.
